How we got here

The ideas that led to modern AI
Rob CornishNanyang Technological University

Some distinctive features of modern AI

1

It can produce different answers to the same question.

2

Often even the people who built it cannot explain its behaviour.

3

It can be wrong with complete confidence.

4

It often tends to agree with you.

To understand these, we need to understand how and why these systems are built as they are.

The history of AI stretches back decades.

Probably you know much of the story already! But we will start at the beginning.

Classical AI

How to write an intelligent computer program?

PROGRAM
“cat”
Why is the sky blue?
Air scatters blue light the most.
Prove or disprove the Riemann hypothesis.
theorem riemann_hypothesis : RiemannHypothesis := by …

Naive attempt: just write the program

mark: 68
IF mark >= 80 THEN "A+" ELSE IF mark >= 70 THEN "A" ELSE IF mark >= 65 THEN "B+" … ELSE "F"
“B3”

ELIZA, 1966: the first chatbot

I need some help, that much seems certain.
PROGRAM
IF they say I need X SAY WHAT WOULD IT MEAN TO YOU IF YOU GOT X IF they say … my mother … SAY TELL ME MORE ABOUT YOUR FAMILY IF they say my mother X me SAY WHO ELSE IN YOUR FAMILY X YOU …
WHAT WOULD IT MEAN TO YOU IF YOU GOT SOME HELP
Perhaps I could learn to get along with my mother.
TELL ME MORE ABOUT YOUR FAMILY
My mother takes care of me.
WHO ELSE IN YOUR FAMILY TAKES CARE OF YOU

ELIZA's implementation was based on explicit rules

What about a program that detects cats?

IF … AND … THEN …
“cat”

Two problems arise:

  1. 1The world is fuzzy
  2. 2The rule is too hard to write

Problem 1: the world is fuzzy

Where does it stop being a cat?

Problem 2: the rule is too hard to write

To a computer, a photo is a grid of pixels, often many millions.

So the rule would have to look something like this:

IF pixel[1] > 142 AND pixel[2] < 87 AND pixel[3] > 120 … millions more lines … THEN “cat”

Probability

An approach to uncertainty

Instead of a single answer, return a bag of possible answers.

Ambiguous inputs should get less confident bags.

This helps with fuzziness. But how do we write this program?

Learning

Instead of writing one program, search a space of programs

Every dot is a different program.

Instead of writing a program directly, we write a search procedure for finding a good one.

The same works when the programs give bags instead of single answers.

How can we obtain a space of programs?

Let's start with a single program to illustrate.

We can view the number 104 as a knob to turn.

We can vary the program by adjusting the knob.

A program can have many knobs.

Each setting of the knobs gives one program.

Adjusting the knobs moves to a different program.

The key problem in machine learning is basically: how to find a good setting for these knobs?

Modern AI is based on neural networks

1998
60 thousandLeNet-5 reads handwritten digits
2012
60 millionAlexNet recognises photos
2020
175 billionGPT-3 writes text
2026
nearly 3 trillionthe largest openly published models

The knobs of a neural network are called weights. These determine what the program does.

How many programs are there?

about 10843 billion
settings of the weights in GPT-3 (2020)
1080
atoms in the observable universe

A price we pay: loss of interpretability

IF mark >= 80 THEN "A+" ELSE IF mark >= 70 THEN "A" ELSE IF mark >= 65 THEN "B+" … ELSE "F"

We "know" the full program, but we cannot easily understand it.

How do we search the space of programs?

This search process is called training

Method 1: learn from examples

After many examples, the program hopefully learns what to do.

Problem: what does it do with something different?

It will still output something, and may hallucinate an answer confidently.

Outputting a bag does not necessarily help either.

How else can we search the space?

Method 2: learn from interactions with the world

Connect the program to actions that affect the world

Define a reward quantifying how "good" each outcome is.

For example: a race where the goal is to reach the finish.

One possible reward gives a point for each green target the boat hits.

We let the program act and measure the reward.

We then tune the knobs to improve the reward.

We then repeat. Eventually, the program hopefully learns to reach the finish.

Problem: specifying rewards can be difficult

Misspecified rewards lead to misaligned behaviour.

Generating

Programs can generate data

Previously our program took a picture as input and gave a bag of labels

We can also reverse this process: given a label, we can produce a bag of pictures.

To "run" this program, we can sample from the bag of pictures.

Usually we get a different sample every time, even with the same input.

How can we obtain such a program?

We can compare its bag with a bag of real examples, and tune the knobs to make them more alike.

The pace of progress has been especially vivid

2014digits, 28 × 28 pixels
2014faces, 48 × 48
2015bedrooms, 64 × 64
2017faces, 1024 × 1024
2022“a photograph of an astronaut riding a horse”
2022“photograph of a polar bear in the desert”
2024a valley at sunset, from a one-sentence description

Goodfellow et al. 2014 · Radford et al. 2015 · Karras et al. 2017 · Stable Diffusion, DALL·E 2 · FLUX

A natural extension of this task

Mask part of an image, and return a bag of possible completions.

The same idea is possible with text inputs

A program of this form is a language model. This is the core of modern AI.

In practice, we output one token at a time

Usually a token is a subword rather than a whole word.

Let's take stock

This is the core of modern AI: huge language models trained to output bags of possible next words.

But it doesn't stop here.

Moonshot AI, Kimi K3 technical report (2026)

Modern AI

How do we make these systems useful?

Why is the sky blue?
PROGRAM
Air scatters blue light the most.
Write a function that finds the average mark.
def average(marks): return sum(marks) / len(marks)
Prove that √2 is irrational.
theorem irrational_sqrt_two : Irrational (√2) := by …

More is needed for this. But modern AI research has developed many such ideas.

An example task: summarisation

Volcanoes form where molten rock, called magma, rises through cracks in the Earth’s crust. Most are found at the edges of tectonic plates. As the magma rises, gas pressure builds until it erupts as lava, ash and gas.
PROGRAM
Volcanoes erupt where magma rises through the crust, mostly at plate edges.

We want a program that takes a paragraph, and gives back a short summary.

How can we use a language model for this?

…after three weeks of failed attempts, it turned out the thermometer had been reading two degrees high the whole time. Lesson learned: calibrate first. TL;DR: our results were wrong because the thermometer was faulty.
…so in the end we moved the whole department to the new building over the holidays, and only lost one box of test tubes. TL;DR: the move went fine.
…which is why the committee has decided to postpone the trip until the spring, when the weather should be more reliable. TL;DR: the trip is moving to spring.

TL;DR means too long; didn't read. Often it is followed by a short summary.

There are presumably many examples of this pattern on the internet.

Building a summariser from a sentence completer

Volcanoes form where molten rock, called magma, rises through cracks in the Earth’s crust. Most are found at the edges of tectonic plates. As the magma rises, gas pressure builds until it erupts as lava, ash and gas. TL;DR:
Volcanoes erupt where magma rises through the crust, mostly at plate edges.

Having trained a sentence completer, we can obtain a summariser "for free".

Example output: GPT-2 (2019)

Prehistoric man sketched an incredible array of prehistoric beasts on the rough limestone walls of a cave in modern day France 36,000 years ago. Now, with the help of cutting-edge technology, those works of art in the Chauvet-Pont-d’Arc Cave have been reproduced to create the biggest replica cave in the world. … TL;DR:
The original site in Vallon-Pont-D’arc in Southern France is a Unesco World Heritage site and is the oldest known and the best preserved cave decorated by man. The replica cave was built a few miles from the original site in Vallon-Pont-D’Arc in Southern France. The cave contains images of 14 different species of animals including woolly rhinoceros, mammoths, and big cats.

Radford et al., “Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners” (2019), Table 14

A decent summary, despite never being taught to summarise.

Other examples of useful behaviour

Chemistry

Sodium hydroxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to give water and sodium chloride.

Physics

A stone is dropped from rest. Ignoring air resistance, after two seconds it has fallen about 20 metres.

Arithmetic

347 + 586 = 933

This works surprisingly well, but not perfectly.

Many tasks require more than sentence completion

Write a short poem about the sea.
Use a word that describes your favorite sea creature.
Write an essay about the sea.
Write a story about a sea creature.
Write a personal essay about the sea.

Here the model should actually write a poem, not just complete the sentence.

One approach: fine tuning with examples

Adjust the knobs to match explicit examples of how to answer in these cases

Early chatbots used answers people rated highly. An unintended consequence was sycophancy.

Another approach: reward correct behaviour

Give it a question whose answer can be checked.

Adjust the knobs to encourage correct answers, and repeat.

In practice it is better to allow the model to output reasoning tokens before answering.

This works for verifiable problems, e.g. maths and code. More subjective domains (e.g. writing) are harder.

Another idea: give the model tools

Like with humans, it can be difficult for a language model to reason in its head.

To help, we can give it access to tools via a harness.

The model writes a tool call, and the harness runs it and returns the result.

The model can then decide what to do with the result.

A language model in a harness connected to tools is called an agent.

A challenge: context is limited

Over time, an agent accumulates a large context

There is a limit to how much context a model can handle.

If this limit is exceeded, the context must be compacted. Doing this well is hard.

A new frontier: multi-agent systems

In addition to calling tools, agents can communicate with each other.

With hundreds of agents, what they do together is very hard to predict.

Summary

Some distinctive features of modern AI, explained

1

It can produce different answers to the same question.

It writes by drawing from a bag, one word at a time.Generating
2

Often even the people who built it cannot explain its behaviour.

Its program is billions of knobs, found implicitly by a search procedure.Learning
3

It can be wrong with complete confidence.

There is nothing to constrain its behaviour outside the examples it has seen.Learning
4

It often tends to agree with you.

Post-training can reward answers that people approved of.Modern AI
